meta.title: Who really said "Hitler didn't snub me; it was our president who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jesse Owens really said it — at a Republican rally in Kansas City on 15 October 1936, campaigning for Alf Landon. A United Press flash printed it the next morning.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1913–1980 · American sprinter and long jumper; four gold medals, Berlin 1936
answer.sourceLine: Owens said it at a Republican campaign rally in Kansas City, Missouri, on the night of 15 October 1936, while stumping for Alf Landon against Franklin D. Roosevelt. A United Press flash datelined Kansas City the next morning carries the line word for word on page one of The Waterbury Democrat, 16 October 1936 ↗ — a contemporaneous report, not a later recollection.

source.excerpt: OWENS SORE — Kansas City, Mo., Oct. 16 — (UP) — Jesse Owens, Negro Olympic track star, told an audience of 1,000 Negroes here last night that it was President Roosevelt and not Feuhrer Hitler who snubbed him during the recent Olympic games in Berlin. “Hitler didn’t snub me — it was our president who snubbed me,” Owens said at a republican rally. “The president didn’t even send me a telegram.”
trail: 4 September 1936 — Owens declares for the Republican ticket. The McDowell Times, page 1 ↗: “Owens Jumps Into Political Ring; Landon for President,” datelined New York, Sept. 2.

15 October 1936 — Owens tells an audience of about a thousand at a Kansas City Republican rally that it was Roosevelt, not Hitler, who snubbed him. A United Press flash carries the line to press the next morning, on page one of The Waterbury Democrat ↗.
2007 — the line reaches most modern readers through Jeremy Schaap’s Triumph, p. 211, which is the citation Wikiquote ↗ attaches to it.
Afterwards — the thought resurfaces in Owens’s better-known formulation about not being invited to shake hands with Hitler or with the President, carried by ESPN SportsCentury ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Library of Congress OCR of page 1; the OCR reads “Feuhrer”. The racial terminology is the newspaper’s own, retained here because this is a period document.

author.name: Jesse Owens
author.heading: Who was Jesse Owens?
author.metaLine: 1913–1980 · American sprinter and long jumper; four golds at the 1936 Berlin Olympics
author.bio: James Cleveland “Jesse” Owens (12 September 1913 – 31 March 1980) won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — the 100 m, 200 m, long jump and 4×100 m relay — in front of Adolf Hitler. He came home to a ticker-tape parade up Broadway and to a country that still made him ride the freight elevator at the Waldorf Astoria to reach a reception held in his honour. That autumn he took the stump for the Republican presidential nominee, Alf Landon, and it was from a Landon platform, not from a memoir, that this line was first heard.

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: The words are genuinely Owens’s — that part survives scrutiny. What almost never survives the trip is the setting. Strip the date and the podium away and a line of election-year politics reads like a wise old champion’s late-life verdict, which is not what it was.

items.who: Quote pages that print the line bare, with no date or place
items.why: It was said at a partisan political event during a presidential campaign. Wikipedia places it at a Republican rally in Kansas City on 15 October 1936 — Jesse Owens, Wikipedia ↗ — and the United Press flash the next morning confirms the rally and the audience of about a thousand.

items.who: Anyone using it as proof that Hitler shook Owens’s hand
items.why: Owens is contrasting two slights, not describing a handshake. His own 1936 account, as recorded on Wikiquote ↗ citing The New York Times of 25 August 1936, is that Hitler rose and waved as Owens passed his box, and Owens waved back.

items.who: Modern renderings that run it together as one flowing sentence
items.why: The 1936 wire text sets it as two separate quoted sentences with the reporter’s attribution between them, and uses a dash rather than a semicolon: “Hitler didn’t snub me — it was our president who snubbed me,” Owens said at a republican rally. “The president didn’t even send me a telegram.” See the page-one scan ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Owens said it, and a newspaper printed it within about twelve hours — on the front page of The Waterbury Democrat for 16 October 1936 ↗. The only thing usually missing is that he said it while campaigning for the other candidate.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By October 1936 the “Hitler snubbed Jesse Owens” story had been running in American papers for two months. Owens’s answer was not a defence of Hitler; it was an attack on his own president, delivered from a partisan podium. He had declared for the Republican nominee, Alf Landon, that September — “Owens Jumps Into Political Ring; Landon for President,” The McDowell Times, 4 September 1936 ↗ — and was being paid to do campaign outreach among Black voters.

The rally line landed because it was true in the way that stung: Roosevelt never invited Owens to the White House and never publicly congratulated him. Owens had been cheered by a hundred thousand Germans, handed a paper bag with ten thousand dollars in it during his Broadway parade, and then sent up a freight elevator at the Waldorf Astoria. The telegram that never came was the smallest possible gesture, and its absence was the point.
context.detailsSummary: The fuller record: what Owens said about Hitler in 1936, and how he put it later
detailsBody: On the alleged snub itself, Owens’s contemporaneous account was that nothing had happened. Wikiquote ↗ records him saying — citing The New York Times of 25 August 1936 — that Hitler had to leave the stadium early, that Owens passed near his box on the way to a broadcast, and that the Chancellor rose and waved, and Owens waved back.

The same thought later hardened into the sentence most people can quote today: “I wasn’t invited to shake hands with Hitler, but I wasn’t invited to the White House to shake hands with the President, either,” as carried by ESPN SportsCentury ↗. That version is the reflective one. The 1936 version, the one on this page, was campaign ammunition.
context.pull: Owens wasn’t defending Hitler. He was running down Roosevelt — from a Republican platform, three weeks out from a presidential election.

sourcesVerified.claim: Page 1 of The Waterbury Democrat, 16 October 1936, carries a United Press item headed "OWENS SORE", datelined Kansas City, Mo., Oct. 16, containing the words: "Hitler didn't snub me —it was our president who snubbed me," Owens said at a republican rally. "The president didn't even send me a telegram." It also states Owens told an audience of 1,000 there "last night".
The Library of Congress catalogue record identifies this issue as The Waterbury Democrat (Waterbury, Conn.), October 16, 1936, and supplies a Chicago-style citation for it.

Wikiquote's Jesse Owens page lists the quotation "Hitler didn't snub me; it was our president who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram." in its 1930s section, citing Jeremy Schaap, Triumph: The Untold Story of Jesse Owens and Hitler's Olympics (2007), New York: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, p. 211. The same page also records Owens's 1936 statement "Mr. Hitler had to leave the stadium early... he arose, waved his hand at me and I waved back at him," citing The New York Times, August 25, 1936, p. 25, and gives Owens's dates as 12 September 1913 – 31 March 1980.

Wikipedia's Jesse Owens article states that on October 15, 1936, Owens addressed an audience of African Americans at a Republican rally in Kansas City, remarking: "Hitler didn't snub me—it was our president who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram." It also states that FDR never invited Owens to the White House, that Owens endorsed Alf Landon and did campaign outreach for him, and that Owens was made to use a freight elevator at the Waldorf Astoria after his ticker-tape parade.

Page 1 of The McDowell Times (Keystone, W.Va.), 4 September 1936, carries an article headed "Owens Jumps Into Political Ring; Landon for President", datelined New York, Sept. 2, reporting that Jesse Owens would campaign for Governor Alf M. Landon, the Republican presidential nominee.

ESPN SportsCentury's "Owens pierced a myth" carries Owens's statement: "I wasn't invited to shake hands with Hitler, but I wasn't invited to the White House to shake hands with the President, either."

The Internet Archive record identifies Triumph: The Untold Story of Jesse Owens and Hitler's Olympics as by Jeremy Schaap, published Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 2007 (ISBN 9780618688227). The item itself is access-restricted, so its page 211 text was not read.
Quote Investigator has no article investigating this quotation; a site search for "Jesse Owens" returns only two unrelated articles about "Find the good and praise it".
